name: Central banks vs energy inflation
backstory: The Iran war cut oil supply and pushed up [[headline inflation]], so central banks have been trying to work out whether the price jump fades by itself or leaks into wages and services. Euro area inflation reached 4%, the Bank of England hiked to 4%, and the Fed sits at 3.875%, which is barely above US inflation.
today: Traders are now leaning toward a 25 basis point Fed hike next month, because the Fed's preferred inflation gauge rose 3.8% in October and third-quarter GDP was revised up to 4.3%, which means the economy is strong while prices are hot. President Trump called the GDP revision a record setting error that should be investigated, which shows how politically sensitive strong data has become when it argues for higher rates. In Europe, the ECB's consumer survey showed people perceive inflation at 4.1%, the highest since July 2024, and Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos won the backing needed to succeed Christine Lagarde next year. At home, shoppers are hunting for value, toys are getting pricier, and the average new car hit a record $51,109 in October.

name: AI trade jitters
backstory: The biggest AI-linked tech firms make up so much of the S&P 500 that doubts about AI hit the whole market. After Nvidia's CEO left on Nov 12, stocks sold off, official papers warned that AI [[valuation]]s look stretched, and the index fell four straight weeks before Nvidia's board approved Jensen Huang's return and the Nasdaq jumped 6.51% on Monday.
today: Tech led a broad rebound, with the Nasdaq up 2.31%, and headlines described the best week in over a year for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, as investors took a break from AI jitters. Even so, Nvidia is still down nearly 28% for November and 21% for 2026, so the week's gains only repaired part of the damage. Huang is also heading to Capitol Hill, which shows how political the company's China and chip story has become. The ECB's latest financial stability review also lists AI adoption and the way AI spending is increasingly paid for with debt as things to watch.

name: US midterms and the dollar
backstory: After the midterms produced what headlines call a Democratic rout, investors asked how divided government might change tariffs, spending and the dollar. The dollar then had its biggest rally since 2024 and hit a 20-month high, though headlines credited hawkish Fed bets and not the election.
today: The dollar index rose 0.33% to 104.01 as Treasury yields climbed and traders priced in a possible 25 basis point Fed hike next month, and it is on track for its longest monthly winning streak in two years. Washington also planned a fresh round of tariffs on 14 trading partners while offering lower rates to countries that sign trade deals, which keeps pressure on those partners. There is also a newer explanation going around for why the dollar tends to bounce after sharp stock selloffs, tied to how foreign owners of US stocks protect themselves against currency swings.

name: Iran war and oil
backstory: The conflict began in early 2026 and cut global oil output by 12 million barrels a day in March, but prices stayed below records because stored oil filled the gap. The IEA says the Hormuz shock lifted the world's oil and gas import bill 25% to $1.6 trillion.
today: WTI fell 0.72% to $83.08 as a stronger dollar and the possibility of more OPEC+ output offset worries about supply, with the market waiting for the weekend OPEC+ meeting on 2027 policy. Brent still notched its first weekly gain in November after attacks on tankers, so the supply risk has not gone away. Fuel costs are hurting businesses too, as budget airline Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy after failing to secure funding while fuel costs soared.

name: Yen defense
backstory: A weak yen pushed Japan to intervene [sell dollars to buy yen] in the currency market, including a record $50 billion in one day. The BOJ's 1.25% rate is 2.625 percentage points below the Fed's 3.875%, which encourages selling yen to hold dollars. Japan's economy unexpectedly shrank in Q3 as energy costs bit.
today: USD/JPY was 159.32, down 0.04%, so the yen was little changed. The BOJ chief played down soft consumption data and signaled a near-term rate hike. Japan's inflation accelerated, and the country posted a sixth straight monthly trade deficit. A Reuters-style analysis says BOJ ambiguity on the path of hikes could tempt yen bears. In Friday's Asian session, the Nikkei fell 2.9% on chip and metals stocks.
